segments.text: Hello, everyone. We are continuing with our introduction to photonics video series with
lecture number two. Lecture number two deals with the wave behavior of light. We've seen
in the first lecture that light represents an electromagnetic wave or a form of electromagnetic
energy that has both wave and particle properties. In this lecture, we are going one step further
and analyzing some of the specific phenomena that can be explained only if you're looking at the
light as a wave. So we are going to be analyzing a few phenomena related to the light, specifically
reflection, refraction, and then also we are going to establish a few laws, specifically law of
reflection and so-called Snell's law of refraction that will be used to quantify the behavior of
light as a wave in the case of behavior when the light hits another medium or propagates from one
medium into the other medium, etc. And finally, at the end, we're also going to talk a little bit
about the diffraction and interference, which are also the phenomena that pertain to light
wave behavior. With this slide, we're introducing another quantity that is related to the wave
behavior, so-called phase. As already mentioned, waves exhibit a certain wave behavior that can
be represented by the sinusoidal curve as shown on the plot on this slide. And that wave behavior
or that sinusoidal behavior is both in a time domain and in a space domain. In other words,
we have a vibration both in time and space. Another way to represent the wave behavior is
in terms of so-called phase where on the x-axis instead of units of length or units of time,
we are putting the units of angles and we see that the total period
is equal to be correlated to the phase of 360 degrees. So by doing this type of correlation,
we can remove the dependence of the x-axis from time and space and look at everything in terms
of angles, which greatly simplifies the whole mathematical analysis of these types of
behaviors that can be described by sinusoidal curves. So we can define the phase of a wave as
the angular displacement of a specific point on the sinusoidal curve from the last positive
zero crossing of the wave, where a positive zero crossing occurs at those zero displacement points
where the new displacement is about to become positive. All these are the properties of
sinusoidal functions that can further be elaborated to the concepts of trigonometry
that's going to go beyond this class. Now why is the phase as a quantity important for us?
If you compare the two waves that you are seeing on this slide, you can see that both of these

We would use the term coherent to describe multiple light waves that are all in phase or in step

this slide. As you can see, the peaks of all these different six waves are basically occurring
at the same location if you are dealing with the sinusoidal curves that are represented as a

an overall wave of a much greater amplitude with very, very high peaks and lower valleys.
So in other words, they are perfectly synchronized. It's almost like we are creating a
perfect storm that consists of all these different waves. We will see that coherent light

power than the coherent light that's produced from laser sources. So to summarize,
